statement:
Progress in AI is not only about making models larger. It is also about making computation more useful.

Neryva exists to study how large-scale AI systems can use computation more effectively, train more stably, and deploy more reliably under real constraints. This is not a narrow optimization problem. It is a research agenda that touches architecture, training dynamics, inference systems, and deployment engineering.

The prevailing approach to capability gains in AI has relied heavily on scale: more parameters, more data, more compute. This approach has produced remarkable systems, but it has also created real problems. Training runs are fragile. Inference is expensive. Deployment is constrained by hardware, latency, and cost. And many of the gains from scale come with waste — computation spent on redundant activations, unstable training regimes that need constant intervention, and inference pipelines that do not adapt to the actual difficulty of the task.

Neryva's research agenda is organized around the belief that these problems are not secondary. They are central to making AI systems that actually work at scale, in the real world, under real constraints. We study routing, sparsity, training stability, and inference optimization not because they are fashionable, but because they are the technical mechanisms through which efficiency, stability, and deployability are achieved.

The lab's work is grounded in measurement, not aspiration. We focus on problems where progress can be demonstrated, where claims can be tied to evidence, and where the research is legible enough for others to build on.
